# A density-sandwich inequality at the weighted centroid

## Theorem

Let B be a convex body in R^d, d>=1. Let eta be a finite measure with
0<=eta<=1_B dx, and let g be the centroid of

    rho=1_B dx+2eta.

Then every closed halfspace H containing g satisfies

    |B intersect H|+eta(H)
        >=(gamma_d/2)(|B|+2eta(B)),
    gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.                                (1)

No regularity, log-concavity, or prescribed support shape of eta is
assumed. Domination makes eta absolutely continuous with density between
zero and one. The result is a continuous auxiliary theorem, not by itself
the full mixed-integer conjecture.

## 1. Normalize and use cap-root concavity at the centroid

Divide every measure by |B|. Write kappa for uniform probability on B and
continue to write eta for the divided submeasure, so eta<=kappa. Put
a=eta(B). The desired inequality becomes

    s+r >= (gamma_d/2)(1+2a),
    s=kappa(H), r=eta(H).                               (2)

It suffices to prove this for the parallel halfspace whose boundary passes
through g. The original containing halfspace includes that one. Because
rho has density at least one relative to kappa, its centroid is in int(B):
every supporting affine functional has a strictly smaller average than its
maximum. Thus the through-centroid cap has 0<s<1. Boundary hyperplanes
have zero kappa and eta mass, so their weak or strict endpoint conventions
cause no ambiguity here.

Fix its unit normal u, and let X=u.x denote the scalar projection. Define
the normalized tail volume and its root on the projection interval by

    U(t)=kappa{X>=t},      G(t)=U(t)^(1/d).

G is concave. For two thresholds, the Minkowski combination of the two
corresponding caps lies in the intermediate cap of B; Brunn-Minkowski gives
the asserted root concavity. All sets are convex and compact, and the
endpoint values follow by continuity.

The projection law of kappa has a continuous strictly increasing cumulative
distribution on its support interval: interior sections of the positive
body have positive (d-1)-volume, and hyperplanes have zero d-volume.
Consequently U(X) is uniformly distributed on [0,1] under kappa. In d=1
this is simply the uniform interval formula. Since eta<=kappa, its
pushforward by U has a density h(v) in [0,1] relative to dv.

The centroid identity and Jensen applied to G under the probability
(kappa+2eta)/(1+2a) give

    (1+2a)s^(1/d)
       >=d/(d+1)+2 integral_0^1 v^(1/d)h(v)dv.          (3)

Moreover integral h=a and integral_0^s h=r, since the cap is X>=u.g.

## 2. The exact bathtub reduction

For an increasing function v^(1/d), a density between zero and one of
prescribed mass on an interval minimizes its integral by filling the
leftmost subinterval. This follows by subtracting that indicator: the
difference has nonpositive values before the cutoff and nonnegative values
after it, while its total integral is zero. Subtracting the cutoff value
of the increasing function makes the weighted difference nonnegative.

Apply this separately to [0,s] and [s,1]. Put q=1+1/d. Then

 integral_0^1 v^(1/d)h(v)dv
   >=(1/q)[r^q+(s+a-r)^q-s^q].                         (4)

The relevant intervals fit because 0<=r<=s and 0<=a-r<=1-s.
Equations (3),(4) imply

    q(1+2a)s^(q-1)
       >=1+2r^q+2(s+a-r)^q-2s^q.                      (5)

Set

    U=1/s,       E=r/s,       Q=(s+a-r)/s,
    phi(t)=t-[d/(d+1)]t^(1+1/d),       c=1/(d+1).

Thus U>=1, 0<=E<=1, 1<=Q<=U. Direct division of (5) by q s^q gives

    phi(U)+2phi(Q)+2phi(E)>=2c.                        (6)

For clarity, one can check the algebra using
F(t)=t^q-q t+q-1: (5) is equivalent to
F(U)+2F(Q)+2F(E)<=3/d; since F/q=-phi+c, this is (6).

## 3. A scalar Fenchel inequality

Put

    k=1/gamma_d=(1+1/d)^d,     h0=2k-2,     A0=2+2k.

We prove that (6) implies

    U+2Q-h0 E<=A0.                                    (7)

For any real t and z>=0, elementary one-variable maximization gives

    phi(z)+t z <= c(1+t)_+^(d+1).                     (8)

Indeed for t>-1 the derivative vanishes at z=(1+t)^d,
which is the unique maximum by concavity. For t<=-1 the maximum is zero
at z=0. Take tau=1/d. Applying (8) with t=tau to U,Q and with
t=-tau h0/2 to E yields

 phi(U)+2phi(Q)+2phi(E)+tau[U+2Q-h0 E]
   <=3c(1+tau)^(d+1)+2c(1-tau h0/2)_+^(d+1).         (9)

By (6), it is enough to verify that the right side of (9) is at most
2c+tau A0. After multiplying by d(d+1) and collecting terms, this is
exactly

    2d[1-(k-1)/d]_+^(d+1)
        <=4d+2-(d+1)k.                               (10)

Here are explicit bounds in every dimension. The binomial theorem gives
k>=2. Also log(1+1/d)<1/d gives k<e, and e<11/4. One elementary upper
bound for the latter is

    e=sum_(j=0)^infinity 1/j!
      <=8/3+(1/24)sum_(j=0)^infinity 5^(-j)
       =87/32<11/4.

For d>=3 the right side of (10) is therefore greater than
(5d-3)/4, which is at least d. On the other hand

 [1-(k-1)/d]_+^(d+1) <=(1-1/d)^(d+1)<1/2.

For the last inequality, the binomial estimate
(1+1/(d-1))^(d-1)>=2 shows (1-1/d)^(d-1)<=1/2, and the remaining square
factor is strictly less than one. Thus the left side of (10) is less
than d, proving (10) for d>=3.

For d=2, k=9/4. The left side of (10) is 27/128 and its right side is
13/4. For d=1, k=2, and the two sides are zero and two. This proves (10)
and hence (7) in every case.

## 4. Recover the cap inequality

The identity a=s(Q+E-1) gives

    (1+2a)/s=U+2Q+2E-2.

Equation (7) therefore says

    (1+2a)/s<=2k(1+E)=2k(s+r)/s.

Multiplying by s/(2k) proves (2). Undoing the measure normalization proves
(1) for every through-centroid halfspace, and hence every containing
closed halfspace.

The proof tracks the coefficient gamma_d/2 exactly. It uses no localization
assertion about extremal profiles, and its scalar condition was derived
directly from the actual cap-root concavity and the density domination.
